eng-reading-quiz-container:Passage 1.baslik: Passage 1 — A branch librarian addresses a city council
eng-reading-quiz-container:Passage 1.html: (1) Members of the council, I have worked at the Eastside branch for nineteen years, and I have never once asked this body for anything. (2) I am asking now. (3) The proposal before you would close our doors at five o'clock instead of nine. (4) On paper, that saves four hours a day. (5) In our reading room, it erases the only hours when a night-shift nurse can help her son with algebra, when a man who drives a delivery van can finish the résumé he cannot type on his phone, when a girl whose apartment has no quiet corner can study for her exams. (6) You will hear that these patrons can simply come earlier. (7) They cannot; that is precisely why they come late. (8) I do not doubt that the budget is tight. (9) I ask only that, before you balance it, you count the people who will pay for the savings.

eng-reading-quiz-container:Passage 2.baslik: Passage 2 — From an essay on navigating a city
eng-reading-quiz-container:Passage 2.html: (1) My grandfather navigated Istanbul by landmarks: the bakery with the green awning, the mosque whose minaret leaned slightly toward the sea, the corner where the tram bell always rang twice. (2) I navigate it by a blue dot. (3) The dot is never wrong, and that is exactly the problem. (4) Because it never fails, I never have to notice anything; because I never notice anything, the city has become, for me, a series of instructions rather than a place. (5) I am not proposing that we throw away our phones. (6) Maps on screens have saved me from more wrong turns than I can count. (7) But a tool that removes every chance of getting lost also removes the chance of finding what we were not looking for.

eng-reading-quiz-container:Passage 3.baslik: Passage 3 — From an address on communication in engineering
eng-reading-quiz-container:Passage 3.html: (1) In 1999, NASA lost the Mars Climate Orbiter because one team's software reported thruster data in imperial units while another team's software expected metric units. (2) The mathematics on both sides was sound; what failed was the agreement about what the numbers meant. (3) The failure lived in the space between the teams. (4) Engineering students often imagine that the hard part of their future work will be the mathematics. (5) It will not be. (6) The hard part will be making sure that what you mean is what your colleague understands—across departments, across languages, across time zones. (7) Learn your equations, by all means. (8) Then learn to write a sentence that cannot be misread.

eng-writing-quiz-container:Draft 1.baslik: Draft 1 — Student proposal: water refill stations
eng-writing-quiz-container:Draft 1.html: (1) Every day, the vending machines in our cafeteria sell bottled water to students who could drink it for free. (2) Last month, the student council counted the empty bottles in the recycling bins near the cafeteria: about 1,400 in a single week. (3) Refill stations, which filter tap water and display how many bottles they have saved, cost less than many people assume. (4) A nearby school installed two stations last year. (5) Its weekly bottle count fell by more than half within one semester. (6) Our school should get refill stations. (7) Some students worry that tap water tastes worse, but the stations filter the water before it reaches the spout.

eng-writing-quiz-container:Draft 2.baslik: Draft 2 — Student research paragraph: urban trees
eng-writing-quiz-container:Draft 2.html: (1) On a summer afternoon, an asphalt parking lot can be far hotter than a shaded park only a few streets away. (2) Multiplied across a whole city, such hot surfaces produce what scientists call the urban heat island effect: cities stay warmer than the countryside around them. (3) Trees reduce this effect in two ways: their canopies block sunlight before it reaches the pavement, and they release water vapor that cools the surrounding air. (4) I personally love trees because they are beautiful. (5) Cities that have expanded their tree cover have reported lower surface temperatures in newly planted neighborhoods. (6) Planting trees, therefore, is not merely decoration; it is public-health infrastructure.

eng-writing-quiz-container:Draft 3.baslik: Draft 3 — Student email to a university admissions office
eng-writing-quiz-container:Draft 3.html: (1) Hey! (2) I'm a high school student in Istanbul and I'm super interested in your Mechanical Engineering program. (3) I have completed AP Calculus AB, and I am currently studying AP Physics C: Mechanics. (4) I would like to know whether AP scores can be used to meet any of the program's admission requirements. (5) Thanks a lot!!

eng-writing-quiz-container:Draft 4.baslik: Draft 4 — Student argument: bike lanes on Elm Avenue
eng-writing-quiz-container:Draft 4.html: (1) Some shop owners on Elm Avenue argue that the proposed bike lanes will hurt their businesses by removing parking spaces. (2) This concern deserves a serious answer. (3) Bike lanes always increase sales for every shop on the street. (4) Cyclists tend to spend less per visit than drivers. (5) They visit more often, so their total monthly spending can be similar or higher. (6) The city council will vote in March. (7) The vote will decide whether the lanes are built.

eng-writing-quiz-container:Draft 5.baslik: Draft 5 — Student essay for the school science magazine: a repair club
eng-writing-quiz-container:Draft 5.html: (1) Every June, the hallway outside the physics lab fills with abandoned equipment: calculators with cracked screens, headphones missing one ear, a desk lamp that flickers like a nervous candle. (2) Most of these objects are not broken beyond saving. (3) They are broken beyond our patience. (4) A repair club, meeting once a week in the lab, would teach students to diagnose faults, to solder loose connections, and replacing worn batteries safely. (5) The club would also save the school money, the equipment budget has been cut twice in three years. (6) Our teachers have offered to supervise. (7) What we need now is a room, a toolbox, and a willingness to look at a broken thing and ask how it works.

eng-writing-quiz-container:Draft 6.baslik: Draft 6 — Student lab-report abstract: the speed of sound
eng-writing-quiz-container:Draft 6.html: (1) In our experiment, we measured the speed of sound in air using a resonance tube partly filled with water. (2) By raising and lowering the water level, the first two resonance positions were located for a 512 Hz tuning fork. (3) The distance between these positions equals half a wavelength, so the wavelength was 0.67 m. (4) Multiplying the wavelength by the frequency gave a speed of 343 m/s, which is real close to the accepted value at room temperature. (5) Our result has a small uncertainty. (6) The largest source of error was judging by ear exactly where the sound was loudest. (7) Future groups could reduce this error by using a microphone connected to a data logger.

eng-reading-quiz-container:Passage 4.baslik: Passage 4 — From an essay on reading and leisure (original, written in a nineteenth-century style)
eng-reading-quiz-container:Passage 4.html: (1) It is a common complaint of our age that men have no leisure; yet I suspect the truer complaint would be that they have leisure enough, and know not what to do with it. (2) The merchant who rises before the lamplighter has finished his rounds will tell you that he has not an hour to call his own; but follow him of an evening, and you shall find him turning the pages of three newspapers, each of which informs him of the same fire, the same election, and the same misfortune at sea. (3) He is not idle, he will protest; he is keeping himself acquainted with the world. (4) I do not quarrel with the newspaper. (5) It is a useful servant, and a nation that could not read of its own affairs would soon cease to have any affairs worth reading of. (6) But a servant who is suffered to sit at the head of the table will in time forget that he is a servant. (7) The mind, like the stomach, is not nourished by the quantity it receives but by the portion it digests; and he who swallows the whole of the day's intelligence before breakfast may find himself, by supper, as hungry and as ignorant as he began. (8) Consider the farmer of my boyhood, who owned four books and had read each of them, I believe, a dozen times. (9) He could not have told you the price of cotton in Liverpool, but he could reason upon any question you put to him with a steadiness that would have shamed a parliament. (10) His knowledge was narrow, but it was his own; ours is broad, and it belongs to the printer. (11) I would not have my reader burn his papers, nor retire to a hillside with four volumes and a cow. (12) I would only ask him, before he takes up the next sheet, to put to himself a plain question: what will I know when I have finished it that I shall still know at the end of the week? (13) If the answer be nothing, let him lay it down, and take a walk, or take up a book that has survived its author; for the hours he saves will be the only leisure he has ever truly possessed.

eng-reading-quiz-container:Passage 5.baslik: Passage 5 — From remarks delivered at a public meeting
eng-reading-quiz-container:Passage 5.html: (1) Last July, on the hottest afternoon of the year, two thermometers sat four kilometers apart in our city. (2) The one on Değirmen Street, beneath a row of sixty-year-old plane trees, read 31 degrees Celsius. (3) The one in the parking lot behind the new shopping center, where the trees had been removed to make room for 400 additional spaces, read 39. (4) Eight degrees is not a statistic; it is the difference between an afternoon an elderly person can survive at home and one she cannot. (5) Researchers have measured this effect in cities around the world, and the pattern is consistent: on the hottest days, neighborhoods with dense tree cover are several degrees cooler than neighborhoods without it. (6) In our own city, the municipal health office reported that of the 23 heat-related hospital admissions last summer, 17 came from the three districts with the least tree cover. (7) Critics of the proposed planting program raise two objections, and both deserve an answer. (8) The first is cost: the program would spend roughly 14 million lira over five years. (9) That is a real sum. (10) But it is less than the city spent last year repaving roads that buckled in the heat—roads that, under shade, would have lasted longer. (11) The second objection is time: a sapling planted today will not shade anyone for a decade. (12) This is true, and it is precisely the reason to begin now. (13) The plane trees on Değirmen Street were not planted by people who expected to sit beneath them. (14) They were planted by people who understood that a city is not the possession of a single generation but a loan held in trust for the next. (15) The council will vote on the planting program next month. (16) I ask each member to stand, before that vote, for ten minutes in each of those two places, and then decide.

eng-reading-quiz-container:Passage 6.html: (1) My father kept a drawer he called "the hospital." (2) Into it went the radio with the loose dial, the lamp that flickered, the toaster that browned only one side of the bread. (3) On Sunday afternoons he would open the drawer, choose a patient, and spread its parts across the kitchen table on a sheet of newspaper. (4) Not every patient survived. (5) But I learned, watching him, that a machine is not a sealed mystery; it is a set of decisions someone made, and decisions can be understood. (6) That lesson is harder to learn today, and not because children are less curious. (7) Many of the devices we own are glued rather than screwed together; their batteries cannot be replaced without special tools; their manuals, if they exist at all, advise the owner to "contact an authorized service provider." (8) Manufacturers defend these designs, and some of their reasons are sound: a sealed phone resists water, and a thinner case is lighter in the hand. (9) Yet a design that keeps water out can also keep the owner out, and the second effect is rarely advertised. (10) The cost is not only the price of a new device when the old one could have been mended. (11) It is the slow disappearance of a habit of mind—the expectation that when something breaks, one might look inside and find out why. (12) A society that loses that expectation does not merely throw away more toasters. (13) It becomes a society that accepts, a little more readily each year, that the workings of things are someone else's business. (14) I am not nostalgic for the flickering lamp. (15) I am nostalgic for the Sunday afternoon, for the newspaper spread across the table, and for the quiet assumption, which my father never thought to put into words, that understanding was something an ordinary person was allowed to attempt.

eng-reading-quiz-container:Passage 7.baslik: Passage 7 — From an argumentative essay on public benches
eng-reading-quiz-container:Passage 7.html:
(1) When the city removed the benches from Kordon Square last spring, the official explanation was maintenance: the wood was splitting, and repairs would cost more than the budget allowed. (2) No one held a ceremony for the benches, and few people complained. (3) Yet within a month, the square had changed. (4) The elderly men who had played backgammon there every afternoon moved to a café two streets away, where a table cost the price of a tea. (5) Mothers with strollers paused, looked around, and kept walking. (6) The square had not lost its fountain or its plane trees; it had lost its reason to stay.

(7) We tend to judge public spaces by what they contain—a statue, a playground, a stage for summer concerts. (8) We should judge them instead by what they permit. (9) A bench is a modest object, but it grants a remarkable permission: to remain in public without buying anything, without a destination, and without explaining oneself to anyone. (10) Few other places in a modern city extend that permission so freely.

(11) The case against benches deserves to be taken seriously. (12) Benches must be cleaned and repaired, and some officials worry that they attract people who sleep or linger for hours. (13) These are real costs, and a city that ignored them would be careless. (14) But the remedy for a broken bench is a repaired one, and the remedy for a person with nowhere to sleep is not the removal of the last place where he may sit. (15) To solve a social problem by taking away furniture is to mistake the symptom for the disease—and to punish everyone else in the process.

(16) I am not asking the city to cover every pavement with seating. (17) I am asking that, before any bench is removed, someone ask who uses it and what they will do instead. (18) The answer, more often than not, will be that they go home, or go somewhere that charges for the privilege of sitting down. (19) A city that cannot offer its citizens a free place to rest has quietly decided that they are welcome only while they are spending money.

eng-reading-quiz-container:Passage 8.baslik: Passage 8 — From an address at the opening of a town waterworks (original, written in a nineteenth-century style)
eng-reading-quiz-container:Passage 8.html:
(1) Fellow citizens, I am aware that many of you came here this morning less to celebrate than to inspect, and I honor you for it. (2) It was your money that dug these trenches and laid these pipes, and a man who has paid for a thing has every right to look it over before he praises it. (3) I ask only that, while you inspect, you also remember. (4) Remember the summer of the fever, when the carts went through our streets at dawn and no family on Mill Lane could say with confidence that it would be whole by evening. (5) Remember that the physicians of that season, learned and devoted as they were, could do little more than sit beside the dying, for the cause lay not in any sickroom but in the well at the corner, from which rich and poor alike drew their water. (6) We did not know it then. (7) We know it now.

(8) There were those who told us that the work was too costly, that a town of our size had no business with reservoirs and filtering beds, that such things were for great cities with great revenues. (9) I do not dismiss them; they spoke from prudence, and prudence is a civic virtue. (10) But I would ask them to set the cost of these pipes beside another account—the wages lost in the weeks of sickness, the orphans maintained at public charge, the trade that fled our market while the fever stayed. (11) Measured against that ledger, the waterworks is not an extravagance. (12) It is the cheapest thing we have ever bought.

(13) And let no one suppose that the benefit stops at our own doorsteps. (14) The child who drinks clean water today will labor tomorrow, and pay his share of the rates, and raise children of his own who need never learn the word we learned that summer. (15) What we have built is not a convenience for this generation alone; it is a debt paid forward to people whose faces we shall never see.

(16) I will not detain you longer. (17) The valves are ready, and the water is waiting. (18) Inspect it, by all means—and then drink.

eng-writing-quiz-container:Draft 7.baslik: Draft 7 — Student letter to the town council: restoring the night ferry
eng-writing-quiz-container:Draft 7.html:
(1) Until 2021, a ferry crossed the bay between Kuzey Harbor and the town center every hour until midnight. (2) That year, to save money, the transit authority ended all service after 8 p.m. (3) The council is now reviewing the transit budget for next year, and it should restore late-evening ferry service on Fridays and Saturdays.

(4) Without the late ferry, residents of Kuzey Harbor who work evening shifts in the town center have few good options for getting home. (5) The road around the bay is 38 kilometers long, and the last bus leaves at 9:15 p.m. (6) A taxi costs about 900 lira, which is more than many restaurant workers earn in a shift. (7) Ferries are an old form of transportation that people have used for thousands of years. (8) Some workers have told me that they now leave their jobs early or turn down weekend shifts altogether.

(9) The late ferry would also help businesses. (10) In a survey our class conducted of 40 restaurants and shops near the town pier, 31 owners said that their evening sales had fallen since 2021. (11) Several owners mentioned that customers from Kuzey Harbor no longer come for dinner because they cannot get home afterward. (12) Weekend evenings are when these businesses usually earn the most.

(13) Some council members, who obviously do not care about working people, argue that late-evening ferries carry too few passengers to justify their cost. (14) It is true that ridership on the last ferries was lower than during the day. (15) The transit authority estimates that restoring four late crossings each Friday and Saturday night would cost 1.2 million lira per year. (16) But that figure does not account for the fares those passengers would pay, and it does not include the income that workers and businesses are losing now.

(17) In conclusion, the ferry is important. (18) The council should bring it back.

eng-writing-quiz-container:Draft 8.baslik: Draft 8 — Student article for the school magazine: the Svalbard seed vault
eng-writing-quiz-container:Draft 8.html:
(1) In a mountain on the Norwegian island of Spitsbergen, roughly 1,300 kilometers from the North Pole, sits a building whose narrow concrete entrance looks like the door to a military bunker. (2) Inside, at a constant temperature of minus 18 degrees Celsius, the Svalbard Global Seed Vault stores more than one million samples of crop seeds, deposited by gene banks from around the world. (3) Its purpose is simple: if a war, a natural disaster, or a disease destroys a crop variety somewhere else, a backup copy will survive in the Arctic cold.

(4) Seed banks matter because the world's food supply depends on surprisingly few varieties. (5) Over the past century, farmers in many countries have increasingly planted a small number of high-yield varieties, and thousands of traditional varieties that were once common have disappeared from fields. (6) Those traditional varieties often carry traits, such as resistance to drought or to particular pests, that modern breeders may someday need. (7) A seed bank, in other words, is less like a museum and more like an insurance policy.

(8) The vault has already been used in a real emergency. (9) In 2015, researchers whose seed collection near Aleppo had been disrupted by the war in Syria withdrew samples they had deposited in Svalbard. (10) They used the samples to rebuild their collection at new research stations in Lebanon and Morocco. (11) This was the first withdrawal in the vault's history.

(12) Seed banks have limits. (13) Seeds stored in a freezer do not change along with new pests and climates the way seeds planted in fields do, generation after generation. (14) For this reason, many scientists argue that seed banks should support, not replace, the work of farmers who keep traditional varieties growing in their own fields.

(15) Seed banks are really important and stuff, and everyone should know about them. (16) Svalbard was opened in 2008.

eng-reading-quiz-container:Passage 9.baslik: Passage 9 — From a speech by a city water engineer to an international forum on urban resilience (original, written for practice)
eng-reading-quiz-container:Passage 9.html:
(1) Thank you for inviting me, though I suspect I am the least glamorous speaker on your program. (2) The architects before me showed you towers that bend in the wind and parks that float on rivers. (3) I have come to talk to you about pipes. (4) More precisely, I have come to talk about the pipes no one has looked at in sixty years, because they are underground, because they still work, and because no mayor has ever cut a ribbon in front of a repaired valve.

(5) In my city, we lose roughly one liter of every four we treat before it reaches a single tap. (6) It escapes through cracks the width of a fingernail, through joints that have shifted a few millimeters with every season of frost and thaw. (7) No single leak is dramatic. (8) Together they amount to a river flowing quietly into the soil beneath our streets—a river we pay to clean, pump, and then lose.

(9) You may be thinking that this is a local problem, a matter for budget committees rather than an international forum. (10) I would have thought so too, once. (11) But the cities represented in this room are spending billions on new reservoirs, new desalination plants, new sources of water to meet growing demand. (12) Some of that demand is real. (13) Some of it, I would argue, is simply the water we already have, escaping through systems we have neglected. (14) Building a new reservoir to feed a leaking network is like buying a larger bucket for a roof you refuse to fix.

(15) I do not say this to scold anyone. (16) Maintenance is unpopular for understandable reasons. (17) Its successes are invisible: when we replace a corroded main, the result is that nothing happens—no flood, no boil-water notice, no headline. (18) Its costs, meanwhile, are visible and immediate, measured in torn-up streets and detoured buses. (19) A politician who funds maintenance pays the price today for a disaster that, if she succeeds, no one will ever know was avoided.

(20) So I want to propose a different way of keeping score. (21) Let us count the crises that did not occur. (22) Let us publish, alongside the photographs of new bridges, the number of kilometers of pipe renewed this year and the liters of water no longer lost. (23) Let us give the inspector with the flashlight the same applause we give the architect with the model. (24) A city is not only what it builds; it is also what it keeps from falling apart.

(25) When I began this work, an older engineer told me that the best compliment our department could ever receive was silence. (26) For many years I believed him. (27) Today I am asking you to break that silence—not with complaints, but with attention.

eng-reading-quiz-container:Passage 10.baslik: Passage 10 — From an essay by a literary translator (original, written for practice)
eng-reading-quiz-container:Passage 10.html:
(1) Every few months, a list appears online of "untranslatable words" from the world's languages. (2) There is the Portuguese saudade, a longing for something absent; the Japanese komorebi, sunlight filtering through leaves; the Turkish yakamoz, the glimmer of light on the night sea. (3) The lists are charming, and I confess I read every one. (4) But I have spent twenty years translating novels for a living, and I have come to think that the idea behind them is not only mistaken but quietly condescending.

(5) Consider what the word "untranslatable" claims. (6) It suggests that a feeling or an image belongs so completely to one language that speakers of other languages cannot reach it. (7) Yet the lists themselves disprove this: each entry is followed by an English explanation that most readers understand perfectly well. (8) What the lists actually show is that English lacks a single word for these things—a much smaller claim, and a much less interesting one. (9) English also lacks a single word for "the day after tomorrow," which Turkish calls öbür gün and German calls übermorgen, but no one concludes that English speakers are unable to think about the future.

(10) The condescension lies in what the lists imply about the people who use these words. (11) They are presented as possessing mysterious sensibilities—the melancholy Portuguese, the nature-loving Japanese—as though a vocabulary were a national personality. (12) The fisherman in İzmir who says yakamoz is not having a more poetic experience of the sea than a fisherman in Maine; he simply has a quicker way of saying what he sees.

(13) None of this means translation is easy. (14) It is, in fact, endlessly difficult, but the difficulty rarely lives in single words. (15) It lives in rhythm, in jokes, in the weight a sentence carries because of everything a culture has said before it. (16) When a character in a Turkish novel says "Kolay gelsin" to a man repairing a roof, the phrase means something like "May it come easily to you," and I can translate those words in a second. (17) What takes me a week is deciding whether an English reader will hear in it the ordinary courtesy that a Turkish reader hears, or a strange, almost biblical blessing.

(18) So I would like to propose a different list—one not of words that cannot be translated, but of moments when translation asks us to pay attention. (19) Such a list would be longer and less pretty. (20) It would not flatter anyone's sense of the exotic. (21) But it would describe what actually happens when one language reaches toward another: not a wall, but a long and patient conversation.

eng-reading-quiz-container:Passage 11.baslik: Passage 11 — A letter from a restaurant chef in Seoul to a former apprentice who has just opened her own kitchen (original, written for practice)
eng-reading-quiz-container:Passage 11.html:
Dear Mina,

(1) Your letter arrived on a Tuesday, which in our kitchen is the day we make stock, so I read it standing beside the big pot with the onions still in my hands. (2) Congratulations. (3) I mean that more than the single word can carry. (4) Opening a kitchen of your own is the bravest foolish thing a cook can do, and I have never been prouder of anyone who left me.

(5) You ask for advice, and I am suspicious of advice, including my own. (6) When I was your age, an old chef in Busan told me that a cook should taste everything three times: once to know it, once to judge it, and once to forgive it. (7) I thought he was being poetic. (8) It took me ten years to understand that he was being practical. (9) The first taste tells you what the dish is. (10) The second tells you what it lacks. (11) The third—this is the hard one—tells you whether the lack is the dish's fault or yours, whether you are tasting the soup or your own tiredness, your own pride, your memory of how your mother made it.

(12) You will be tired, Mina. (13) There will be nights when the dining room is half empty and a critic you respect writes that your food is "competent," which is the cruelest word in our language. (14) On those nights you will be tempted to change everything—to add truffle to the rice, to make the plates louder. (15) Do not. (16) Or rather, do not do it that night. (17) Taste the dish the next morning, when you have slept and the critic's word has lost some of its heat, and change only what the third taste tells you to change.

(18) I know you will think this is the caution of an old man who has stopped taking risks. (19) Perhaps it is. (20) But the risks I regret are not the dishes I left alone; they are the ones I ruined because I could not bear to be called ordinary for one more week. (21) A menu built from panic tastes like panic. (22) Customers cannot name it, but they feel it, the way you can feel that a house has recently been in an argument.

(23) One last thing, and then I will go back to my onions. (24) Write down the first dish you cook in your new kitchen exactly as you made it, every gram and every minute. (25) In ten years, you will cook it again, and you will learn more from the distance between those two plates than from anything I could tell you.

With pride and a little envy,
Chef Yoon

eng-reading-quiz-container:Passage 12.baslik: Passage 12 — "Let Us Fix What We Own," an editorial from a regional newspaper (original, written for practice)
eng-reading-quiz-container:Passage 12.html:
(1) Somewhere in your home there is probably a drawer of dead electronics: a phone whose battery gave out, a tablet with a cracked screen, a pair of headphones that stopped charging after eighteen months. (2) Most of these devices are not broken in any serious sense. (3) They have a single failed part that could be replaced in minutes—if the manufacturer allowed it.

(4) Increasingly, manufacturers do not. (5) Batteries are glued rather than screwed into place. (6) Replacement parts are sold only to authorized repair shops, if they are sold at all. (7) Some devices are programmed to display warning messages when an independent technician installs a part, even a genuine one. (8) The result is that repair becomes so expensive or inconvenient that replacement seems like the only sensible choice.

(9) This should concern everyone, not only the hobbyists who enjoy taking things apart. (10) Electronic waste is one of the fastest-growing waste streams in the world, and much of it contains materials that are difficult to recycle safely. (11) Every device thrown away early also represents the energy and raw materials used to make it—mined, refined, shipped, and assembled—discarded along with the cracked screen.

(12) Manufacturers argue that restrictions protect consumers. (13) Untrained repairers, they say, can damage devices or install unsafe batteries, and the companies' reputations suffer when that happens. (14) This concern deserves a serious answer, and it has one. (15) No one is proposing that companies be forced to guarantee repairs they did not perform. (16) The proposal is simply that owners and independent shops have access to the same parts, tools, and manuals that authorized technicians already use. (17) A safe battery does not become dangerous because the person installing it does not wear a company uniform.

(18) Several governments have begun to act. (19) The European Union has adopted rules requiring that certain appliances be designed for repair and that spare parts remain available for years after a model is sold, and some U.S. states have passed similar laws for electronics. (20) Our state legislature will consider such a bill this spring. (21) It should pass.

(22) A generation ago, it was ordinary to take a radio to a repair shop on the corner. (23) We do not need to return to the past to recognize that something useful was lost when fixing things became the exception rather than the rule. (24) Ownership should mean more than the right to throw something away.

eng-reading-quiz-container:Passage 13.baslik: Passage 13 — From a memoir by an astronomer recalling her first job (original, written for practice)
eng-reading-quiz-container:Passage 13.html:
(1) I was twenty-three when I arrived at the observatory, and I believed, with the confidence of someone who had read a great many books, that astronomy was the study of light. (2) Within a week I had learned that it was mostly the study of waiting. (3) The telescope sat on a ridge in the Atacama Desert, where the air is so dry that my lips cracked on the first afternoon and the sky at night was so crowded with stars that the familiar constellations disappeared into it, the way a friend's face disappears into a crowd.

(4) My job was simple and, I thought, beneath me. (5) I was to sit in the control room from dusk until dawn, check the instruments every hour, and record the weather. (6) If clouds came, I was to close the dome. (7) If the humidity rose above a certain number, I was to close the dome. (8) If the wind gusted, I was to close the dome. (9) For the first month I closed the dome more often than I opened it, and I filled the hours between with resentment, which I mistook for ambition.

(10) The person who changed this was Héctor, a night technician who had worked on the ridge for nineteen years and who spoke to the instruments as if they were elderly relatives. (11) One night, when a band of high cloud had stalled over the western horizon and I had nothing to do but complain, he handed me a pair of binoculars and told me to look at the edge of the cloud. (12) "Not at the stars," he said. (13) "At the edge." (14) I looked for a long time before I saw it: the cloud was not still at all but unraveling, thread by thread, as the drier air beneath it pulled it apart. (15) An hour later the sky was clear, and we opened the dome, and the telescope collected light that had left its galaxy before there were humans on Earth to see it.

(16) I would like to say that I understood the lesson at once. (17) I did not. (18) What I understood was smaller: that there was something to watch even when there was nothing to see. (19) It took me years to recognize that this was not a smaller lesson at all, and that most of my career would be spent at the edges of things—at the margins of data sets, in the noise around a signal, in the faint fringe where one kind of light gives way to another.

(20) Héctor retired the year I finished my doctorate. (21) I sent him a copy of my dissertation, which he could not have had much use for. (22) He wrote back a single line: "I hope you are still looking at the edges." (23) I am.

eng-reading-quiz-container:Passage 14.baslik: Passage 14 — From an essay on travel and crowded destinations (original, written for practice)
eng-reading-quiz-container:Passage 14.html:
(1) Each summer, the photographs return: crowds pressed shoulder to shoulder on a Venetian bridge, a line of climbers waiting near the summit of Everest, a beach in Thailand so famous from a film that it had to be closed to let its coral recover. (2) The images are usually accompanied by a familiar complaint about "overtourism," and the complaint usually blames the tourists—their selfies, their cruise ships, their apparent inability to stay home.

(3) I understand the irritation. (4) I have stood in such crowds myself and felt, with no sense of irony, that the other people were ruining my experience. (5) But blaming tourists as a group seems to me both unfair and unhelpful. (6) It is unfair because the desire to see the world is not a vice; for most of history, travel was a privilege of the wealthy, and the fact that millions of ordinary people can now afford a trip abroad is, on balance, something to celebrate. (7) It is unhelpful because shame does not change behavior on the scale that matters. (8) No family planning its one holiday of the year will cancel it because a columnist has called them a swarm.

(9) The more useful question is not why so many people travel, but why they all travel to the same few places at the same few times. (10) Part of the answer is that the places are genuinely extraordinary. (11) But part of it is that we have built systems that funnel attention toward them. (12) Guidebooks rank sights; social media rewards the photograph everyone recognizes; airlines and cruise companies schedule their routes around the most famous ports. (13) A traveler who wants to go somewhere less crowded must work against all of these forces at once.

(14) If the problem is one of distribution, then so are the solutions. (15) Cities can manage how many people enter at peak hours, as some have begun to do with reservation systems and entry fees. (16) Regions can invest in making their less famous towns easier to reach. (17) And travelers, without abandoning their trips, can make small adjustments—arriving in October instead of August, staying three nights in one town rather than one night in three.

(18) None of these measures is a cure. (19) Some of the world's most beloved places will remain crowded, and some residents will continue to feel, reasonably, that their homes have become stage sets. (20) Their frustration deserves attention, and the money tourism brings does not cancel it. (21) But a city overwhelmed by visitors is not a moral failure of the visitors; it is a design problem, and design problems, unlike moral failures, can be solved with planning.

eng-writing-quiz-container:Draft 9.baslik: Draft 9 — Student research essay: restoring mangrove forests (practice draft, written for Meberra)
eng-writing-quiz-container:Draft 9.html:
(1) Along tropical coastlines from Indonesia to Brazil, mangrove trees grow where few other plants can survive: in salty, muddy water that rises and falls with the tides. (2) Their tangled roots, which arch above the waterline like the legs of a table, slow incoming waves and trap sediment. (3) For centuries, coastal communities have depended on these forests for fish, firewood, and protection from storms. (4) Mangroves are cool.

(5) Over the past several decades, however, large areas of mangrove forest have been cleared for shrimp farms, rice paddies, and coastal construction. (6) When the trees disappear, the shoreline behind them becomes more exposed. (7) Storm surges travel farther inland, and the young fish that once sheltered among the roots have nowhere to grow. (8) Shrimp is one of the most popular seafoods in the world.

(9) In response, many countries have launched replanting programs. (10) Some of these programs have succeeded. (11) Others have failed, and the reasons are instructive. (12) In several projects, volunteers planted seedlings in mudflats where mangroves had never grown, because the land was easy to reach and available. (13) The seedlings died. (14) Scientists who study restoration now emphasize that mangroves must be replanted where the tides, salt levels, and sediment suit them, usually in areas where they grew before. (15) In some cases, simply restoring the natural flow of water allows mangroves to return on their own.

(16) Mangrove restoration also matters for the climate. (17) Mangrove soils store large amounts of carbon, and when the forests are cleared, much of that carbon can be released. (18) Protecting the forests that remain, therefore, may be just as important as planting new ones.

(19) In conclusion, mangroves are important, and we should plant more of them.

eng-writing-quiz-container:Draft 10.baslik: Draft 10 — Student opinion piece for the school newspaper: a "library of things" (practice draft, written for Meberra)
eng-writing-quiz-container:Draft 10.html:
(1) Last spring, I needed a sewing machine for a costume project, and I learned that the cheapest new one cost more than I had saved all year. (2) My neighbor lent me hers, and the costume was finished in a weekend. (3) That experience made me wonder how many things students buy, use once, and then store in a closet.

(4) Some public libraries have begun to answer that question with a "library of things." (5) Instead of only books, these libraries lend objects: power drills, telescopes, camping tents, musical instruments, even cake pans. (6) A library in our own city started a small collection two years ago. (7) According to its annual report, the most borrowed items were a ukulele, a projector, and a soil-testing kit. (8) Our school library should start a library of things too.

(9) The benefits for students would be practical. (10) Many class projects require equipment that families may not own, such as a tripod for a film assignment or a scientific calculator. (11) A lending collection would make these assignments fairer. (12) It would also let students try a hobby, like photography or guitar, without spending money on equipment they might abandon after a month.

(13) Some teachers worry that borrowed items will be lost or broken. (14) This is a reasonable worry. (15) The city library handles it by requiring borrowers to sign a simple agreement and by starting with sturdy, inexpensive items. (16) Our school could do the same. (17) Damaged items could be repaired by the robotics club, which already fixes the school's laptops.

(18) A library of things would cost little to start, since many families would probably donate items they no longer use. (19) The library has always been a place for sharing what one person cannot easily own alone. (20) Lending a tripod is not so different from lending a book.

eng-writing-quiz-container:Draft 11.baslik: Draft 11 — Student report for a world history class: the qanats of Iran (practice draft, written for Meberra)
eng-writing-quiz-container:Draft 11.html:
(1) In the deserts of central Iran, where rain is scarce and rivers are few, towns and farms have survived for thousands of years on water that flows through underground tunnels called qanats. (2) A qanat begins at the foot of a mountain, where water collects underground. (3) From there, a gently sloping tunnel carries the water many kilometers to the fields, using nothing but gravity. (4) Along the way, a line of vertical shafts, which look from above like a row of craters, lets workers remove soil and bring air into the tunnel.

(5) Building a qanat required remarkable skill. (6) Specialized diggers, called muqanni, had to judge the slope of the tunnel precisely. (7) If the slope was too steep, the flowing water would wear away the tunnel walls and cause collapses. (8) If it was too shallow, the water would barely move. (9) Muqanni passed their knowledge from one generation to the next, often within the same families.

(10) Qanats also shaped the way communities lived. (11) Because a single qanat served many households, villages developed detailed rules for sharing water, often dividing it by time so that each farmer received the flow for a set number of hours. (12) The system encouraged cooperation, since everyone depended on the tunnel being maintained. (13) Some qanats are still in use today, and in 2016 several were added to UNESCO's World Heritage List.

(14) Today, many qanats are drying up. (15) Modern pumps can draw groundwater much faster than qanats, and as the water table falls, the older tunnels no longer reach it. (16) It's super sad.

eng-writing-quiz-container:Draft 12.baslik: Draft 12 — Student letter to the city council: shade at bus stops (practice draft, written for Meberra)
eng-writing-quiz-container:Draft 12.html:
Dear Members of the City Council,

(1) My name is Deniz Arslan, and I am a junior at Riverside High School. (2) Every weekday I wait for the number 12 bus at the corner of Fifth Street and Market Avenue, where there is no shelter and no tree. (3) In September, the temperature at that corner regularly feels like 38 degrees Celsius by 3:30 in the afternoon. (4) I am writing to ask the council to plant shade trees and install covered shelters at the city's busiest uncovered bus stops.

(5) Heat is not just uncomfortable. (6) Public health agencies warn that long exposure to high temperatures can cause dehydration, dizziness, and heat exhaustion, especially for older adults and young children. (7) At my stop, I often see a woman in her seventies who waits with an umbrella to protect herself from the sun. (8) Last month, a student from my school fainted while waiting there.

(9) Shade makes a measurable difference. (10) For a science class project, my lab partner and I measured the ground temperature at three bus stops on the same afternoon. (11) At the stop with a mature tree, the pavement was about 12 degrees cooler than at my stop. (12) Trees also absorb rainwater and make streets more pleasant to walk along.

(13) I understand that the council has a limited budget. (14) Trees are cheap. (15) A young tree takes years to provide real shade, so shelters would help in the meantime, while trees would provide long-term cooling that shelters alone cannot.

(16) Thank you for considering this request. (17) Me and my classmates would be glad to help plant trees or present our data at a council meeting.

Sincerely,
Deniz Arslan

eng-writing-quiz-container:Draft 13.baslik: Draft 13 — Student biographical essay: Wangari Maathai and the Green Belt Movement (practice draft, written for Meberra)
eng-writing-quiz-container:Draft 13.html:
(1) In 1977, a Kenyan biologist named Wangari Maathai began encouraging rural women to plant trees. (2) The idea sounded modest. (3) But the women she worked with were facing serious problems: streams were drying up, firewood was harder to find, and soil was washing away from deforested hillsides. (4) Maathai believed that planting trees could address all of these problems at once.

(5) The organization she founded, the Green Belt Movement, paid women a small amount for each seedling that survived. (6) This detail mattered. (7) It gave women a source of income, and it rewarded them not for planting quickly but for caring for the trees over time. (8) Over the following decades, the women of the movement planted tens of millions of trees across Kenya.

(9) Maathai soon realized that environmental problems were connected to political ones. (10) Forests were often cleared because powerful people wanted the land, and ordinary citizens had little power to stop them. (11) She began to speak out against corruption and to defend public land, including a park in the center of Nairobi that the government planned to build on. (12) She was arrested several times. (13) She was beaten during a protest. (14) She continued her work.

(15) In 2004, Maathai became the first African woman to win the Nobel Peace Prize. (16) The Nobel committee recognized her contribution to sustainable development, democracy, and peace. (17) Some people at the time asked what tree planting had to do with peace. (18) Maathai answered that when people fight over shrinking resources such as land and water, protecting the environment helps prevent conflict.

(19) Maathai's life shows that small actions can have big effects. (20) She was a very nice person.
